title: Automated Weather Pipeline for Dhaka
summary: Cloud-native weather intelligence for Dhaka, orchestrated by Prefect, stored on S3 and visualized with Streamlit.
content:
The concept was straightforward: Pull weather data from Open-Meteo → transform and clean it → store as Parquet on S3 → serve it through a Streamlit + Plotly dashboard → orchestrated with Airflow and Prefect.

Simple on paper. Humbling in practice.

Extraction was the easiest part as the Open-Meteo API is generous and well-documented. The real work was in the transform layer. Units matter more than you think. I'm based in Bangladesh. My stakeholders (okay, it's just me, but still) think in Celsius and km/h. The API hands you data in various units depending on what you ask for. So the transformation layer standardizes everything. Celsius for temperature, km/h for wind speed, with a careful normalization pass to handle edge cases like missing hourly readings. Then there's timezones. APIs hand you UTC by default but I needed everything converted to Asia/Dhaka, which Python's zoneinfo handled cleanly.

I could've stored the data as CSV which was fine, but Parquet gives you columnar storage, efficient compression and schema enforcement out of the box. Since I'm dumping data to S3 and reading it back for analysis, that efficiency compounds fast.
And honestly? Pushing data to S3 for the first time hits different. It's not some dummy project on your laptop anymore. It feels like you're building actual infrastructure, real world stuff. Once the ETL was done, I used boto3 and pandas to pull the data directly into Streamlit, then handed it off to Plotly for the chart visuals.

Github link: https://github.com/MahirTB/dhaka-weather-pipeline
See the dashboard: https://dhakaweatherinsight.streamlit.app/

title: IDA Loan Report
summary: Explored the IDA dataset using SQL and built a simple Power BI dashboard
content:
Sourced the 'IDA Statement of Credits and Grants' dataset from the World Bank website. I modeled a relational database and loaded the raw data into SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) as two distinct tables.
Conducted initial exploratory data analysis to understand the database schema and table contents.
Executed SQL JOIN operations to consolidate the tables and establish a comprehensive view of the dataset.
During data validation, I identified an unexpected cardinality issue. I initially assumed a 1:1 relationship between Project ID and Credit Number. However, querying the row counts revealed a one-to-many relationship, where a single Project ID was associated with multiple Credit Numbers.
To handle the resulting duplicates and isolate unique records for accurate analysis, I utilized Common Table Expressions (CTEs).
Aggregated the financial data to analyze the overall distribution of loans on a country-by-country basis.
Calculated the total number of IDA-granted projects allocated to each respective country.
Finally, designed and developed an interactive Power BI dashboard to visualize these metrics and deliver actionable insights.

title: Covid-19 Insights - My First Data Analytics Project
summary: This is my first data analytics project where I've used PowerBI for the first tiime
content:
I downloaded a COVID dataset from Kaggle, and it turned out to be quite extensive. Most columns were fine, but there were null values in some. I decided to clean it up by removing those null columns and started my analysis. While getting total cases and total deaths was straightforward using Power BI, calculating metrics like vaccinations per hundred people and death rates proved to be a bit tricky. The nature of the dataset was such that it provided daily updates, resulting in numerous duplicates. To streamline the data, I undertook manipulations to derive the total population and the number of people vaccinated for each country.

After obtaining the data, I created a new sheet where I calculated the vaccination percentage of people for each country and later used it for visualization.

Next up, I needed to determine the death rate (how many people are dying per hundred cases) for each country. Using DAX, I created a new table specifically to calculate the death rate.

Now that I have all the metrics, I dived into visualization using Power BI and made a dynamic dashboard which shows all the key metrics regarding the pandemic.

Now, if I want to view the data specific to my country, Bangladesh, I can use the country filter. Additionally, I have the flexibility to explore data for any particular year as needed.
